metadata.title: Introduction: Data Integrity, Reproducibility and the ALLEA Code

params.text:
Welcome to This Course

This module addresses one of the most important pillars of modern science: research integrity. It is designed for early-career researchers, PhD students, postdoctoral fellows, and research support staff who work with research data in any capacity.

The module is structured around the European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA, 2023) and covers the full spectrum from day-to-day data management through to recognising and responding to scientific misconduct.

params.alt: Learning Objectives slide

params.text: Understand key concepts in research data management, including data types, lifecycle, and planning tools such as Data Management Plans (DMPs).
Apply the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) to the organisation and sharing of research data.
Identify the legal and ethical requirements for handling personal data in research, including GDPR obligations and participant rights.
Select appropriate data sharing strategies, repositories, and licensing frameworks for research outputs.
Recognise the causes and consequences of low reproducibility and research waste, and identify strategies for improvement.
Define the three forms of research misconduct — Fabrication, Falsification, and Plagiarism (FFP) — and distinguish them from Questionable Research Practices (QRPs).
Apply the principles of responsible reporting and investigation when research misconduct is suspected.
Critically analyse real-world case studies involving data integrity dilemmas and scientific misconduct scenarios.

params.alt: Defining Research Data — types grid

params.text:
Defining Research Data

Research data is defined as any information collected, observed, or created for the purposes of analysis to produce original research results. This is an intentionally broad definition — it encompasses everything from sensor readings and patient records to interview transcripts and software code.

Understanding what counts as data is the first step in building sound data management practice.

Research data can be quantitative (numerical measurements, experimental results) or qualitative (text, images, audio, video). It also includes observational data captured in the field, experimental data produced under controlled conditions, simulation outputs, and derived or compiled data that has been processed from primary sources.

Format refers to the file structure in which data is stored: structured data (databases, spreadsheets), semi-structured data (XML, JSON), and unstructured data (free text, images, audio files). Format decisions affect long-term accessibility and interoperability.

Dataset scale ranges from small (kilobytes to megabytes — typical of survey responses or lab notebooks) to large (gigabytes to petabytes — characteristic of genomics, imaging studies, or large-scale simulations). The size of a dataset directly determines the technical infrastructure, storage solutions, and management protocols required.

Data passes through four sequential phases: raw (as originally collected, unprocessed), cleaned (errors and outliers removed), processed (transformed or normalised), and analysed (interpreted to produce results). Each transition must be documented to ensure reproducibility.

params.text:
The Research Data Lifecycle

Good data management is not a one-time action — it is a continuous, regenerative cycle that governs data from the moment a study is conceived until long after its findings are published. Understanding this lifecycle allows researchers to plan their workflows proactively rather than scrambling to organise data retrospectively.

Before any data is collected, researchers must define: what data will be collected, in what format, and how it will be stored and protected. This stage produces a Data Management Plan (DMP), which serves as the roadmap for all subsequent stages.

Data is collected according to the protocol defined in the DMP. During this active phase, researchers apply consistent file naming conventions, version control, and quality checks to prevent errors from entering the dataset.

Processed data is subjected to statistical or qualitative analysis to produce findings. This stage must be fully documented so that the analytical pathway can be retraced and verified by independent researchers.

After analysis, data must be preserved in a manner that guarantees its long-term integrity. This includes selecting appropriate repositories, applying encryption for sensitive data, and documenting retention periods in accordance with institutional and legal requirements.

Well-managed data does not end with one study — it becomes a resource for future research. At this stage, data is made discoverable through repositories and catalogues, with appropriate access controls and licences that govern how others may use it.

params.alt: Value of Data Management — key benefits

params.text:
Why Data Management Matters

Effective research data management is not bureaucratic overhead — it is a core scientific competency that directly determines the quality, reproducibility, and impact of research outcomes.

Structured data management processes — consistent naming, version control, and quality checks at each lifecycle stage — prevent errors from compounding. A single mislabelled file or unrecorded data transformation can invalidate an entire study's findings.

When data, analysis scripts, and metadata are well-documented and preserved, other researchers can independently verify results. This is the operational foundation of scientific reproducibility — arguably the single most important quality criterion in empirical research.

Clearly organised, well-documented datasets can be shared with collaborators across institutions and borders without loss of meaning. This is increasingly important in large interdisciplinary and multi-site research projects.

The vast majority of European and international research funders — including the European Commission's Horizon programmes — now mandate the submission of a DMP at the outset of a funded project, and open data sharing by default at project close.

Maintaining rigorous records protects individual researchers in the event of questions about data provenance, authorship disputes, or allegations of misconduct. A complete and well-maintained audit trail is the researcher's strongest defence.

Data deposited in discoverable repositories attracts higher citation rates. Research that is open and reproducible is increasingly preferred by high-impact journals, creating direct career benefits for researchers who invest in good data practice.

params.question: Which of the following is a direct consequence of poor research data management?

answers.text: Difficulty reproducing study results by independent researchers

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Poor data management — missing documentation, unlabelled files, undisclosed transformations — is one of the leading causes of irreproducible research.

answers.text: Lower publication fees in open-access journals

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Publication fees are unrelated to data management quality.

answers.text: Increased statistical power in analysis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Statistical power is determined by sample size and study design, not data management practices.

answers.text: Automatic compliance with GDPR

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. GDPR compliance requires specific legal and technical measures; good file management alone does not ensure compliance.

params.text:
The Data Management Plan (DMP)

A Data Management Plan is a formal, living document that describes how research data will be handled during and after a project. It is required by most European funders and is increasingly demanded by research institutions as a condition of ethics approval.

The DMP is not a bureaucratic formality — it is the operational blueprint that protects both the research and the researchers throughout the project lifecycle.

The DMP begins by describing what data will be collected or generated: the types, formats, volumes, and sources of data expected. This forces researchers to think carefully about scope before data collection begins.

The plan specifies the methodologies, instruments, and quality assurance procedures that will be used. Documenting these standards at the outset ensures that data collection is consistent across the team and over time.

The DMP details where data will be stored during the active project phase, including backup frequency, redundancy (e.g., 3-2-1 backup rule), and security measures. It identifies who has access to the data and under what conditions.

Researchers must specify which data will be shared, when, and through which channel. Where data cannot be shared (e.g., due to personal data protection requirements or commercial confidentiality), the DMP must justify this restriction explicitly.
The DMP identifies how data will be preserved after project completion — including the choice of repository, the retention period, and the file formats chosen for long-term accessibility.
The plan names the individuals responsible for data management at each stage, ensuring clear accountability across the research team and preventing critical tasks from falling through the cracks.
The DMP explicitly addresses any ethical approvals required, consent frameworks for participant data, and compliance with applicable data protection legislation (e.g., GDPR).

metadata.title: FAIR Principles for Scientific Data Stewardship

params.text:
The FAIR Principles

The FAIR principles, first published in 2016, provide an internationally recognised framework for maximising the value of research data. FAIR is not synonymous with 'open' — data can be FAIR while still being access-controlled. The principles apply to both data and the metadata that describe it.

Data must be discoverable by both humans and machines. This requires: a globally unique and persistent identifier (such as a DOI), rich metadata that describe the data comprehensively, and registration or indexing in a searchable resource. The metadata must include the identifier of the data they describe.

Once found, data and metadata must be retrievable using standardised, open protocols. The protocol should allow for authentication and authorisation where necessary. Critically, metadata should remain accessible even when the data itself is no longer available — this ensures that provenance records are maintained indefinitely.

Data must integrate with other datasets and work seamlessly with applications and workflows. This means using formal, broadly applicable languages for knowledge representation, using vocabularies that follow FAIR principles themselves, and including qualified references to related data and resources.

The ultimate goal of FAIR is to enable data to be used and built upon in future research. Data must have rich, accurate metadata, be released with a clear and accessible data usage licence, be associated with detailed provenance information, and meet domain-relevant community standards for data format and description.

params.question: According to the FAIR principles, what must remain accessible even if the original data is no longer available?

answers.text: The metadata describing the data

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Metadata must remain accessible permanently, ensuring that provenance records are preserved even if the underlying data is removed or restricted.

answers.text: The raw data files

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Raw data may be restricted or removed for legitimate reasons; it is the metadata that must remain permanently accessible.

answers.text: The analysis code used to process the data

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Code preservation is good practice, but it is not what the FAIR accessibility principle specifically requires to remain accessible.

answers.text: The published paper reporting the results

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Publication accessibility is a separate issue from FAIR data principles.

params.alt: Organising Data — file naming and version control
README and Metadata — 15-item checklist

params.text:
Organising Your Data

The most sophisticated analysis pipeline cannot compensate for disorganised underlying data. Consistent naming conventions, clear folder structures, and version control are the unglamorous but essential foundations of reproducible research.

Adopt a consistent, descriptive naming convention from the start of a project. Good file names typically include: a project identifier, a date (in ISO 8601 format: YYYYMMDD), a descriptor of the file contents, and a version number. Avoid spaces, special characters, and ambiguous abbreviations. Example: PROJ01_20240315_survey_raw_v01.csv.

Organise files in a logical, hierarchical folder structure that mirrors the research workflow (e.g., /raw/, /processed/, /analysis/, /outputs/). Apply the same structure consistently across all team members. Document the structure in the project README.

Track changes to data files and analysis scripts using version numbers or dedicated version control software (e.g., Git for code). Never overwrite the original raw data — always work on copies. Maintain a change log that records what was modified, by whom, and why.

Every dataset should include a README file in plain text format that enables a new researcher — including your future self — to understand the data without prior context. A complete README includes: project title and description, principal investigator details, date of data collection, geographic location (if relevant), funding sources, licences, description of each file and variable, methodological notes, and any known data quality issues.

Metadata describes your data. Using established metadata standards (e.g., Dublin Core, DDI for social science data, EML for ecological data) makes your dataset interoperable and discoverable. At a minimum, document: the dataset title, creator(s), date of creation, subject keywords, spatial and temporal coverage, data format, and access conditions.

params.question: Which file naming convention is most consistent with best practices in research data management?

answers.text: PROJ01_20240315_survey_raw_v01.csv

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! This name includes a project ID, date in ISO format, content descriptor, version number, and no spaces or special characters.

answers.text: final_FINAL_use this one.csv

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. This name contains spaces and ambiguous version language — classic signs of poor naming practice.

answers.text: data.csv

answers.text: Survey Results March 15.csv

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Spaces in filenames cause problems in many systems, and the date is not in machine-readable ISO format.

metadata.title: Protecting Personal Data: Minimisation, Anonymisation and Pseudonymisation

params.text:
Protecting Personal Data in Research

When research involves data about identifiable human beings, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies in full. GDPR is not an obstacle to research — it is a framework that makes human subjects research ethically sustainable. Violations carry both reputational and significant financial penalties for institutions.

Data minimisation is the principle that researchers should collect only the personal data that is strictly necessary to achieve the study's aims. This is the first and most important safeguard. Before designing any data collection instrument, researchers must ask: 'Do we genuinely need this data point, or are we collecting it because it might be useful later?' Collecting unnecessary personal data creates legal liability and ethical risk without scientific benefit.

Anonymisation is the permanent and irreversible removal of all personally identifiable information (PII) from a dataset. Once properly anonymised, data falls outside the scope of GDPR and can be shared more freely. However, true anonymisation is technically demanding — in practice, re-identification risk must be assessed carefully, particularly for small datasets or those containing rare demographic combinations.

Pseudonymisation replaces direct identifiers with a unique code, while keeping the key that links codes to real identities stored separately and securely. Unlike anonymisation, pseudonymisation is reversible. The dataset remains subject to GDPR, but pseudonymisation is recognised as a technical safeguard that reduces risk. It is appropriate when data must be traceable for clinical or longitudinal purposes.

metadata.title: Three Technical Safeguards for Personal Data

params.question: A researcher permanently removes all personally identifiable information from a dataset so it cannot be traced back to any individual. Which technique has been applied?

answers.text: Anonymisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Anonymisation is the permanent, irreversible removal of PII. Once anonymised, the data falls outside GDPR scope.

answers.text: Pseudonymisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Pseudonymisation replaces identifiers with codes but remains reversible using a separate key — it does not permanently remove the link to the individual.

answers.text: Encryption

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Encryption protects data in transit or at rest but does not remove the identity link — the data can be decrypted and re-identified.

answers.text: Data minimisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Data minimisation means limiting what is collected, not removing identifiers from data that has already been collected.

params.alt: Participant Rights and Informed Consent slide

params.text:
Participant Rights and Informed Consent

The lawful basis for processing personal data in research is typically informed consent. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous. Researchers must also respect the full range of rights that GDPR grants to research participants.

Participants must be told, before data collection begins: the identity of the data controller, the purpose and legal basis of processing, how long their data will be kept, whether data will be shared and with whom, and their rights under GDPR. This information must be provided in plain language, not legal jargon.

Participants have the right to request a copy of all personal data held about them at any time. Researchers must be able to respond to such requests within the legally mandated timeframe (typically one month).

panels.title: Right to Erasure ('Right to be Forgotten')

params.text: Participants retain an unconditional right to request that their data be deleted at any time. This right must be communicated clearly at the point of consent. Researchers must have technical procedures in place to action such requests promptly.

Consent can be withdrawn at any point without consequence to the participant. Withdrawal of consent means the participant's data must be deleted from the dataset, unless the data has already been irreversibly anonymised. Researchers must not make consent a condition for accessing services or benefits.

Personal data may not be kept for longer than is necessary for the stated purpose. The DMP must specify exact retention periods for each data type, justified against the research purpose and any applicable regulatory requirements (e.g., clinical trials data may need to be kept for 25+ years for audit purposes).

params.alt: Data Sharing Strategy — decision checklist

params.text:
Data Sharing and Repository Selection

Sharing research data is increasingly both a scientific obligation and a funder mandate. However, data sharing must be done responsibly — balancing openness with the protection of participants, intellectual property, and commercial interests.

Data should be shared as openly as possible, as closed as necessary. By default, research data produced from publicly funded projects should be made available for reuse. Exceptions must be explicitly justified and documented in the DMP.

A trustworthy research data repository should offer: a persistent identifier (DOI) for each deposited dataset; version control and a preservation commitment; a clear licence policy that governs reuse; appropriate access control mechanisms for sensitive data; and certification (e.g., CoreTrustSeal) attesting to its trustworthiness.

Domain-specific repositories (e.g., GenBank for genomics, PANGAEA for earth and environmental science) are preferred where they exist, as they apply community standards for metadata and formats. Generalist repositories (e.g., Zenodo, Figshare, DANS EASY) accept data from any discipline and are appropriate when no domain repository exists.

Before sharing, verify:

  • Ethics approval covers data sharing
  • Participant consent forms permit the intended sharing
  • All PII has been removed or access is appropriately controlled
  • Third-party data rights have been addressed
  • A licence has been selected
  • A README and data dictionary have been prepared

params.alt: Creative Commons Licences — spectrum diagram

params.text:
Licensing Your Research Data

A licence is the legal instrument that tells users what they can and cannot do with your data. Without a licence, data cannot be legally reused — even if it is publicly accessible. The Creative Commons (CC) licence framework is the most widely used system for licensing research data and outputs.

CC0 ('No Rights Reserved') places the work as fully as possible into the public domain. Anyone can use, share, adapt, and build upon the data for any purpose, without restriction. This is the most open option and is preferred by many funders and repositories for data (as opposed to publications).

CC BY allows anyone to use, share, and adapt the data for any purpose, even commercially, as long as they give appropriate credit to the original creator. This is the standard open licence for most research outputs funded under Horizon Europe.
CC BY-SA requires attribution and additionally requires that any adaptations be shared under the same licence. This 'copyleft' condition ensures that openness propagates through derivatives.

CC BY-NC permits sharing and adaptation with attribution, but prohibits commercial use. This is appropriate when researchers want to enable academic reuse while protecting commercial exploitation of their data.

CC BY-ND allows sharing with attribution but prohibits the creation of derivative works. The data may be distributed but not modified. This is the most restrictive CC licence that still permits sharing.

Without any licence, data is automatically subject to full copyright protection. No reuse is legally permitted without explicit permission from the rights holder. This maximally restricts reuse and is incompatible with most open science mandates.

answers.text: CC BY or CC0

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! CC BY (Attribution) and CC0 (Public Domain) are the most open CC licences and are standard requirements under Horizon Europe open access mandates.

answers.text: CC BY-ND

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. CC BY-ND prohibits the creation of derivatives, severely limiting the reuse potential of the data.

answers.text: CC BY-NC

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. CC BY-NC prohibits commercial use. While appropriate in some contexts, it is more restrictive than required for most Horizon Europe open data mandates.

answers.text: No licence (All Rights Reserved)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. No licence means no reuse is legally permitted, which directly contradicts the funder's open data requirement.

params.alt: Cycle of Research Waste — circular diagram
Overcoming Research Waste — barriers and solutions

params.text:
The Reproducibility Crisis

In 2016, a landmark survey of 1,576 researchers published in Nature found that more than 70% had tried and failed to reproduce another scientist's experiments. More than half had failed to reproduce their own experiments. This is not a minor technical problem — it represents a fundamental challenge to the scientific enterprise and a massive waste of research resources.

Reproducibility: obtaining the same results when re-analysing the same data with the same methods. Replicability: obtaining consistent results when collecting new data using the same methods. Replication: obtaining consistent results across studies using the same or equivalent measurement tools.

Research identifies multiple contributing factors:

  • Selective reporting and publication bias
  • Insufficient statistical power (underpowered studies)
  • Poor data management and inadequate documentation
  • Inappropriate use of statistical methods
  • Lack of pre-registration of hypotheses and analysis plans
  • Pressure to publish novel, positive results ('publish or perish' culture)
  • Inadequate peer review of methods and data

Research waste arises across four interconnected stages: (1) problems with the research question (irrelevant, duplicated, or poorly defined questions); (2) design and methods (inadequate study design, poor control of confounders); (3) execution (poor data collection, loss to follow-up, protocol deviations); (4) reporting (selective reporting, inadequate methods sections, inaccessible data and code).

Researchers who want to improve reproducibility face real systemic barriers:

  • Career incentive structures that reward novelty and publication volume over rigour
  • Journals that prefer positive results
  • Time pressures that discourage thorough documentation
  • Lack of institutional support for open science practices
  • Technical skills gaps (e.g., in statistical methods or data management)

A growing movement towards Open Science addresses the reproducibility crisis through: pre-registration (publishing hypotheses and analysis plans before data collection); open data and open code sharing; pre-print servers for rapid dissemination; registered reports (peer review of methodology before results are known); and institutional recognition of rigorous, reproducible science.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The survey of 1,576 researchers found that over 70% had tried and failed to reproduce another scientist's experiments — a striking finding that catalysed the open science movement.

answers.text: Less than 10%

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The figure was dramatically higher — more than 70% had experienced failed replication.

answers.text: Exactly 50%

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The percentage was substantially higher — over 70%.

answers.text: More than 90%

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The figure was over 70%, not 90%, though even this lower figure represents a serious systemic problem.

metadata.title: Scientific Misconduct: FFP and Modern Predatory Practices

params.text:
The Three Forms of Research Misconduct

The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA, 2023) and most national research integrity frameworks define scientific misconduct as behaviour that falls into one of three categories, collectively known as FFP.

These are not marginal or ambiguous violations — they represent a total failure of research integrity. Each constitutes a serious breach that can result in retraction of publications, loss of funding, institutional investigation, and potential criminal liability.

Fabrication is defined as making up data or results and recording or reporting them as if they were real. This includes inventing experimental outcomes, creating fictitious participants or data points, and generating synthetic results to fill gaps in datasets. Fabrication is the most severe form of misconduct because it introduces entirely false information into the scientific record.

Falsification is defined as manipulating research materials, equipment, or processes, or changing or omitting data or results such that the research is not accurately represented in the research record. This includes: selectively reporting results that support a hypothesis while suppressing contradictory findings; manipulating images beyond acceptable adjustments; altering raw data; and modifying experimental conditions without disclosure.

Plagiarism is defined as using other people's work and ideas without giving proper credit to the original source. This includes copying text verbatim without quotation marks and citation, paraphrasing without attribution, presenting another researcher's ideas or data as one's own, and self-plagiarism (reusing one's own previously published material without disclosure). Plagiarism applies to written text, data, images, code, and all other research outputs.

params.question: A researcher selectively reports only the experimental trials that support their hypothesis, and does not disclose the 40% of trials that produced contradictory results. Which form of misconduct does this represent?

answers.text: Falsification

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Selective omission of data to misrepresent research findings is a form of Falsification — the ALLEA Code specifically includes 'omitting data or results such that the research is not accurately represented'.

answers.text: Fabrication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Fabrication involves inventing data that does not exist. In this case, the data was real — it was selectively suppressed, which constitutes Falsification.

answers.text: Plagiarism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Plagiarism involves misattribution of others' work. This scenario concerns the researcher's own data, not another person's work.

answers.text: A Questionable Research Practice (QRP), not misconduct

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While some forms of selective reporting occupy a grey area, deliberately suppressing 40% of trials to misrepresent results is clearly Falsification under the ALLEA Code.

params.alt: Unacceptable Research Practices — QRP list

params.text:
Questionable Research Practices (QRPs)

Beyond the clear-cut FFP categories, the ALLEA Code of Conduct identifies a range of Questionable Research Practices (QRPs) — behaviours that fall short of outright misconduct but nonetheless undermine research integrity. QRPs are sometimes called the 'grey zone' of research misconduct.

QRPs are particularly insidious because they are often rationalised as acceptable or even normal practice. Understanding them is essential for building a culture of integrity.

panels.title: HARKing — Hypothesising After Results are Known

params.text: Presenting a hypothesis as if it was formulated before data collection when it was actually generated by exploring the data. This misrepresents the confirmatory nature of the analysis and inflates the apparent significance of findings.

Running multiple statistical tests or analyses until a statistically significant result (p < 0.05) is found, then reporting only that result. This exploits random chance to generate false positives and is a leading cause of the reproducibility crisis.

Including individuals as authors who did not make a substantive intellectual contribution ('gift authorship'), or excluding individuals who did ('ghost authorship'). Authorship fraud undermines accountability and misrepresents intellectual ownership.

Submitting the same manuscript (or substantially similar content) to multiple journals simultaneously, or publishing the same findings multiple times without disclosure. This artificially inflates a researcher's publication record.

Failing to maintain complete, accurate, and accessible records of research data, analysis decisions, and protocols. Poor record-keeping makes it impossible to verify or reproduce results and prevents effective investigation of suspected misconduct.

Failing to disclose financial, personal, or professional relationships that could influence the design, conduct, or reporting of research. Transparency about conflicts of interest is a fundamental requirement of research integrity.

params.question: A researcher analyses their dataset six different ways, finds a statistically significant result using one method, and reports only that analysis without disclosing the others. This practice is known as:

answers.text: p-Hacking or data dredging

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Running multiple analyses until significance is found, then reporting only the significant result, is a textbook example of p-hacking — one of the most common QRPs.

answers.text: Fabrication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Fabrication involves inventing data. In this case, real analyses were conducted — the problem is selective reporting of one favourable result.

answers.text: HARKing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. HARKing involves presenting a post-hoc hypothesis as if it were a priori. While related, p-hacking specifically refers to the practice of running multiple tests to achieve significance.

answers.text: Plagiarism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Plagiarism concerns misattribution of others' work — it is not relevant to statistical analysis practices.

params.text:
The Scenario: Professor Brown's Study

Professor Brown has secured a prestigious grant to investigate how environmental and genetic factors impact obesity in urban areas — a large interdisciplinary project combining geographic information systems, Google Street View data, historical hospital records, individual patient lab results, and genetic samples from a biobank.

The team faces an immediate conflict: one researcher insists on uploading all datasets to a public repository, citing a grant mandate for open access under FAIR principles. Others push back, citing GDPR privacy requirements and intellectual property rights.

A deeper investigation reveals that the team has collected a decade's worth of personal patient data — including occupations and residential areas — without ethics committee approval and without informed consent, operating on the assumption that using existing hospital records does not require formal approval.

What specific data management failures allowed the team to harvest personal records without ethical approval? Consider: the role of the DMP, the absence of ethics committee review, and the assumption that 'old data' does not require consent.

The tension between open data mandates (FAIR) and data protection law (GDPR) is real and common. How should a research team navigate this conflict? What does 'as open as possible, as closed as necessary' mean in practice for sensitive health data?

Given that the data has already been collected without proper consent or ethics approval, what steps should the team take now? What are the potential consequences — for the study, the institution, and the researchers — of different courses of action?

params.question: Professor Brown's team collected patient hospital records without ethics committee approval, assuming historical data does not require consent. Under GDPR and research ethics frameworks, this assumption is:

answers.text: Incorrect — ethics approval and informed consent are required for collecting personal health data regardless of whether records are historical

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! GDPR and research ethics requirements apply to the processing of personal health data regardless of the age of the records. Historical data is not exempt from consent and ethics review requirements.

answers.text: Correct — historical records that already exist are exempt from GDPR requirements

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. GDPR applies to any processing of personal data, including historical records. 'Old' data does not lose its legal protection.

answers.text: Partially correct — ethics approval is not needed if a funder mandates open access

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Funder open access mandates concern the publication of research outputs, not the collection of personal data. Ethics approval is always required for collecting personal health information.

answers.text: Correct if the data was anonymised before collection began

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The data was not anonymised before collection — it contained occupations and residential areas. Moreover, anonymisation must occur before or at the point of collection, not retroactively.

params.text:
Case Study 2: Scientific Misconduct

This case study examines a scenario of suspected data falsification in a cell biology laboratory, exploring the ethical and professional dilemmas faced by a lab mentor who discovers evidence of misconduct by a former student and current technician.

The Scenario: Helen and Julie

Helen is a Professor of Cell Biology and lab mentor. Julie is a former graduate student who is now a bitter, uncooperative lab technician — her career setbacks have created significant tensions in the laboratory.

At a lab meeting, Julie presents her latest autoradiography results. She shows a raw data slide from 'Experiment 1', then claims to have independently repeated the process, presenting a second slide representing 'Experiment 2'. Helen notices something physically impossible: the two slides appear to be identical — the cellular structures match perfectly.

params.alt: Case Study: The Confrontation — Suspicion, Denial, Verification, Consensus

params.text:
The Confrontation

The situation unfolds through four stages:

  1. Suspicion: Helen notes that the two slides look identical — a physical impossibility for truly independent experiments.
  2. Denial: Julie claims the slides are from separate experiments with correctly labelled membranes, but states that the original membranes have been 'destroyed'.
  3. Verification: Helen overlays the autoradiography films and finds they match exactly, lacking the idiosyncratic artifacts that would be expected from genuinely independent experiments.
  4. Consensus: Senior scientists who review the evidence agree: it is a duplicated film.

params.alt: Case Study: Critical Evaluation — four discussion questions

params.text: What data management practices, if properly implemented, would have made this type of falsification detectable earlier — or prevented it entirely? Consider: raw data archiving, lab notebook practices, and data audit trails.

panels.title: Discussion Question 2: Guidelines That Should Have Been Employed

params.text: Which specific research integrity guidelines apply to the handling of raw autoradiography data? What does the ALLEA Code of Conduct say about the preservation of original research records and the obligation to maintain data integrity?

How certain must Helen be before she makes a formal accusation? What is the difference between reporting a suspicion and making an accusation? Who should she speak to first — and what institutional channels are available?

panels.title: Discussion Question 4: Cost of a Wrong Decision

params.text: What is the actual cost of a wrong decision — in either direction? Consider: the cost to Julie if the accusation is wrong; the cost to the scientific record, the institution, and the field if the falsification goes unreported; and Helen's professional obligations in both scenarios.

params.question: Helen overlays the two autoradiography films from Julie's 'Experiment 1' and 'Experiment 2' and they match exactly — including idiosyncratic artifacts. Senior scientists agree it is a duplicated film. Which form of research misconduct is most clearly indicated?

answers.text: Falsification — manipulating or duplicating research materials so the data no longer reflects the truth

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Presenting the same autoradiography film as two independent experiments is a clear example of Falsification under the ALLEA Code — research materials are manipulated so the data no longer represents what it claims to represent.

answers.text: Fabrication — making up data or results entirely

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The autoradiography film itself was real; it was presented deceptively as two separate experiments. This is Falsification, not Fabrication (which would involve inventing data from scratch).

answers.text: Plagiarism — using another person's work without attribution

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Plagiarism concerns misattribution of others' intellectual work. Julie's misconduct concerns the manipulation of her own experimental data.

answers.text: A Questionable Research Practice, not formal misconduct

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Deliberately duplicating an experimental result and presenting it as independent replication is unambiguously Falsification — a serious form of research misconduct, not merely a QRP.

params.text:
Principles for Investigating Research Misconduct

When research misconduct is suspected, it must be investigated through a fair, rigorous, and transparent process. The ALLEA Code of Conduct provides 11 core principles that govern how investigations should be conducted. These principles protect all parties involved — including the accused, the accuser, and the integrity of the scientific record.

Anyone who suspects research misconduct has a professional obligation to report it through appropriate institutional channels. Reports should be made in good faith, based on evidence, and without malicious intent. Good faith reporting — even if the allegation ultimately cannot be substantiated — should not result in adverse consequences for the reporter.

Bona fide reporters of research misconduct must be protected from retaliation. Institutions have a legal and ethical obligation to protect whistle-blowers' career prospects, ensure they are not subject to harassment or discrimination, and maintain confidentiality about their identity where possible.

Investigations must be conducted with strict confidentiality to protect all parties — particularly the accused, who must be presumed innocent unless and until misconduct is proven. Premature disclosure of allegations can cause irreparable reputational damage and prejudge the outcome.

The accused has the right to due process: to be informed of the specific allegations, to have adequate time to prepare a response, and to present evidence in their defence. No determination of guilt should be made without this process being followed.

The investigation process itself must be publicly documented — institutions should have clear, published procedures for handling misconduct allegations. Both parties must understand the process, the timeline, and how decisions will be made.

Investigations must be carried to a definitive conclusion. Inconclusive investigations, or cases that are quietly dropped without a formal finding, serve neither justice nor the scientific record. Where misconduct is found, proportionate and transparent consequences must follow.

params.question: A junior researcher reports suspected data fabrication by a senior colleague in good faith, but the investigation ultimately cannot substantiate the allegation due to insufficient evidence. According to research integrity principles, what should happen to the junior researcher?

answers.text: They should be protected from any retaliation — good faith reporting is protected even if the allegation cannot be proven

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Whistle-blower protection applies to good faith reporting regardless of outcome. A report made in good faith based on genuine concern is protected even if evidence is insufficient for a finding of misconduct.

answers.text: They should face disciplinary action for making an unsubstantiated allegation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Disciplinary action would be appropriate only if the report was made maliciously or in bad faith. A good faith report based on genuine concern is protected.

answers.text: They should have their name published alongside the allegation they made

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Confidentiality is a core principle of misconduct investigations — the reporter's identity should be protected, not publicised.

answers.text: They should be barred from making future reports until they can provide stronger evidence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Creating barriers to good faith reporting would undermine the entire misconduct reporting system. Researchers must feel safe to report genuine concerns.

These questions draw on Chapters 13 to 18 — reproducibility and research waste, the definition of misconduct, questionable research practices, the two case studies, and the principles governing investigations. Work through them before moving to the flashcard review and final assessment.

params.question: A postdoctoral researcher is asked by their supervisor to remove three data points that 'look like outliers' from a figure, so the trend appears cleaner. No statistical justification is offered and no record of the removal is kept. How should this be classified?

answers.text: Falsification — manipulating data or omitting results such that the research is not accurately represented

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Removing inconvenient data points without documented statistical justification misrepresents the research record. Legitimate outlier exclusion requires a pre-specified rule and a transparent audit trail.

answers.text: Fabrication — because the resulting figure no longer reflects reality

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Fabrication means inventing data that was never collected. Here real data exists but has been selectively removed, which is falsification.

answers.text: A Questionable Research Practice, since no data was invented

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Undocumented removal of data to change a reported result crosses from the grey zone into falsification — one of the three FFP categories.

answers.text: Acceptable practice, provided the supervisor takes responsibility for the decision

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Seniority does not legitimise data manipulation, and every author carries accountability for the integrity of the reported work.

params.question: During a misconduct investigation, a department head circulates an email to all staff naming the accused researcher and describing the allegation in detail. Which investigation principle has been breached?

answers.text: Confidentiality — the accused must be presumed innocent and protected from premature disclosure

answers.text: Whistle-blower protection — the reporter must be shielded from retaliation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Whistle-blower protection concerns the reporter. Here it is the accused whose position has been prejudiced.

answers.text: Transparency of procedures — the process must be publicly documented

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Transparency requires that the procedure be published in advance; it does not license disclosure of individual case details mid-investigation.

params.question: Which combination of measures most directly addresses the structural causes of the reproducibility crisis, rather than its symptoms?

answers.text: Pre-registration of hypotheses and analysis plans, mandatory data and code deposit, and reform of hiring and promotion criteria to reward rigour over publication count

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The crisis is driven by incentive structures. Pre-registration and open materials constrain QRPs directly, while reforming career incentives removes the pressure that produces them in the first place.

answers.text: Increasing the number of peer reviewers assigned to each manuscript

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. More reviewers may catch more errors, but peer review cannot detect p-hacking or HARKing in the absence of pre-registration and access to the underlying data.

answers.text: Raising the statistical significance threshold from p < 0.05 to p < 0.01

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A stricter threshold shifts the target without removing the incentive to hunt for significance — researchers can p-hack toward any threshold.

answers.text: Requiring all research to be replicated before publication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Universal pre-publication replication is not feasible at scale and does not address why irreproducible work is produced in the first place.

dialogs.answer: Any information collected, observed, or created for the purposes of analysis to produce original research results — including numerical data, text, images, audio, video, and software.
A formal, living document that describes how research data will be collected, organised, stored, shared, and preserved during and after a project. Required by most European research funders.
Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable — a framework of principles for maximising the value and reusability of research data.
The permanent and irreversible removal of all personally identifiable information from a dataset. Once properly anonymised, data falls outside the scope of GDPR.
The replacement of direct identifiers with a unique code, while storing the key separately. Unlike anonymisation, pseudonymisation is reversible and the data remains subject to GDPR.
The GDPR principle that only the minimum personal data strictly necessary to achieve the study's aims should be collected.
Making up data or results and recording or reporting them as if they were real observations.
Manipulating research materials, equipment, or processes, or changing or omitting data or results such that the research is not accurately represented.
Using other people's work and ideas without giving proper credit to the original source. Applies to text, data, images, and code.
Hypothesising After Results are Known — presenting a hypothesis as if it was formulated before data collection when it was actually generated by exploring the data.
Running multiple statistical tests or analyses until a statistically significant result is found, then reporting only that result. A leading cause of the reproducibility crisis.
A continuous, regenerative cycle with five stages: Plan & Prepare → Collect, Organise & Process → Analyse & Interpret → Archive, Store & Secure → Discover, Access & Reuse.

A Creative Commons Attribution licence that permits anyone to use, share, and adapt the data for any purpose, including commercially, as long as appropriate credit is given. Standard for Horizon Europe open access outputs.
A Creative Commons Public Domain Dedication that places work as fully as possible into the public domain with no rights reserved. No attribution is required.
Obtaining the same results when re-analysing the same data with the same methods. Distinct from replicability (new data, same methods) and replication (new data, equivalent tools).
Behaviours that fall short of formal misconduct (FFP) but nonetheless undermine research integrity — e.g. HARKing, p-hacking, gift authorship, duplicate publication.
The institutional obligation to protect researchers who report suspected misconduct in good faith from retaliation, career harm, or harassment — regardless of the outcome of the investigation.

Complete the following questions to demonstrate your mastery of the full course content. These questions draw on all chapters — from data management fundamentals through to research misconduct and investigation.

params.question: A research team is designing a longitudinal clinical study. They plan to collect genetic samples, survey responses, and GPS location data from 500 participants over 5 years. Which of the following best describes a GDPR-compliant approach to this study?

answers.text: Collect only the data strictly necessary, obtain informed consent that specifies the full retention period, pseudonymise all records, and store in a secure access-controlled repository

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! This answer applies all key GDPR principles: data minimisation, specific informed consent, pseudonymisation, and secure controlled storage.

answers.text: Collect all potentially useful data now and decide later what to keep

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. This violates the GDPR principle of data minimisation — only data strictly necessary for the defined purpose may be collected.

answers.text: Anonymise all data at the point of collection, then share it openly without restrictions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Anonymising immediately would prevent longitudinal tracking. GPS and genetic data require pseudonymisation with access controls, not unrestricted open sharing.

answers.text: Store data on personal laptops to prevent institutional data breaches

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Personal laptops without encryption and access controls represent a significantly higher security risk than institutional systems. This approach would violate both GDPR and good data management practice.

params.question: A researcher discovers that a widely cited paper in their field used fabricated data. The paper's findings have influenced clinical practice guidelines. What is the correct first step?

answers.text: Report the suspected misconduct to the researcher's institution through official channels, with documented evidence

params.question: Which of the following actions best demonstrates commitment to reproducible research?

answers.text: Pre-registering the study hypothesis and analysis plan before data collection, then depositing anonymised data and analysis code in an open repository after publication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Pre-registration prevents HARKing and p-hacking; open data and code sharing enables independent verification — together, these represent the gold standard for reproducible research.

answers.text: Reporting only the statistically significant findings and noting that other analyses were 'exploratory'

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Selective reporting of significant results while retroactively labelling others as 'exploratory' is a form of p-hacking — it undermines reproducibility and is a QRP.

answers.text: Keeping data and code private to prevent competitors from replicating the work first

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Withholding data and code actively prevents reproducibility. Open sharing of materials is a core component of responsible science.

answers.text: Running multiple analyses and selecting the one that best supports the intended conclusion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Selecting analyses based on their support for a preferred conclusion is p-hacking — a QRP that directly undermines the reproducibility and trustworthiness of findings.

params.question: A PhD student notices that their supervisor has added a senior colleague as co-author on a paper, despite that colleague having no involvement in the study design, data collection, analysis, or writing. This practice is known as:

answers.text: Gift authorship — a Questionable Research Practice that misrepresents intellectual contribution

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Gift authorship (adding co-authors who made no substantive contribution) is explicitly listed as a QRP in the ALLEA Code and violates international authorship standards (e.g., ICMJE criteria).

answers.text: Appropriate acknowledgement of the colleague's senior role in the department

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Authorship requires substantive intellectual contribution. Senior academic position alone does not qualify someone for authorship under ICMJE or ALLEA standards.

answers.text: A standard academic courtesy with no ethical implications

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Gift authorship has serious ethical implications: it misrepresents who is accountable for the research, and inflates publication records based on relationship rather than merit.

answers.text: Plagiarism, because the colleague's name is being used without their knowledge

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Plagiarism concerns using others' work without attribution. Gift authorship is the opposite problem — attributing authorship to someone who did not contribute.

params.question: The 2016 Nature survey on reproducibility found that more than 70% of researchers had failed to reproduce another scientist's experiments. Which of the following is identified as a primary structural cause of this reproducibility crisis?

answers.text: Publication and career incentive structures that reward novel, positive results over rigorous, reproducible science

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The 'publish or perish' culture, combined with journals' preference for positive results, creates systematic pressure to prioritise novelty over rigour — a primary structural driver of the reproducibility crisis.

answers.text: Intentional misconduct by the majority of researchers

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The vast majority of reproducibility failures reflect systemic pressures and inadvertent errors rather than intentional misconduct. Attributing the crisis to deliberate fraud misses the structural causes.

answers.text: Use of statistics in research — which inherently produces unreliable results

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Statistics, properly applied, are reliable tools. The problem is the misapplication of statistics (e.g., p-hacking) driven by incentive structures, not statistics per se.

answers.text: The internet making it too easy to access and critique other researchers' work

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The internet has actually improved reproducibility by facilitating data sharing, open code, and replication studies. Greater transparency is part of the solution, not the problem.

params.question: A team is writing the Data Management Plan for a three-year project involving interviews with healthcare workers. Which element is most commonly omitted from DMPs, yet is explicitly required?

answers.text: A specific retention period for each data type, justified against the research purpose and any regulatory requirements

answers.text: A list of the software packages the team intends to use

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Software choices are useful context but are not the element most often missing, nor are they a legal requirement of the plan.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A DMP identifies roles and responsibilities, but a full staff roster is neither required nor the common omission.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Publication planning has no place in a Data Management Plan.

Course Complete — Certificate of Completion

Congratulations on completing the Research Data Integrity and Reproducibility module.

You have covered the full spectrum of research integrity — from the fundamentals of data management and FAIR principles, through the ethical and legal dimensions of personal data protection, to the identification and reporting of research misconduct.

The principles you have studied are not abstract ideals — they are operational tools that, applied consistently, protect the quality of science, the welfare of research participants, and your own professional integrity.

Key Takeaways

  • Good data management is a continuous lifecycle, not a one-time task.
  • FAIR principles maximise the value of research data for the entire scientific community.
  • GDPR compliance requires deliberate planning from the very first day of a project.
  • The three forms of research misconduct — Fabrication, Falsification, and Plagiarism — represent a total failure of scientific integrity.
  • Reproducibility is a systemic challenge requiring both individual discipline and institutional change.
  • Reporting suspected misconduct in good faith is a professional obligation — and is protected.
